units.text: Begin with EC2 managed checks on the left. System checks assess underlying infrastructure, instance checks assess the guest, and attached EBS checks assess volume reachability and input and output capability.

Move to application checks. Configure useful HTTP or HTTPS criteria and enable the intended health sources in the Auto Scaling group. A healthy virtual machine does not prove that its application serves requests correctly.

Inspect the custom health panel. Automation can report a result using SetInstanceHealth. Define which failures justify replacing a particular instance before connecting that signal to automatic recovery.
Look at the shared database warning on the right. If every health endpoint depends on one failed database, every server may appear broken. Replacing the fleet will not repair that shared dependency.

With the full slide visible, distinguish diagnosis from response. Supported EC2 recovery addresses certain system failures, while Auto Scaling replacement creates new compute. Match the action to the failure domain.

Follow the draining connection on the left. Load-balancer deregistration delay gives supported in-flight requests time to finish within configured limits. Test the behavior with your actual protocols and request durations.

Move to scale-in protection at the upper right. It controls selection during scale-in, but does not prevent unhealthy replacement, Spot interruption or manual termination. Important work still needs a recovery design.

Follow the queue-worker path. Stop accepting new tasks, finish or checkpoint current work, and make unfinished work available for retry. A successful shutdown preserves work as well as reducing capacity.
Inspect the termination checklist below. Coordinate policies and hooks, then test long requests, failures and deployment-time scale-in. Cleanup must be bounded, and retrying it must be safe.

With the whole slide restored, judge the outcome from the application. Requests should complete or recover, and tasks should remain recoverable. A smaller instance count alone does not prove graceful removal.

Begin with the mixed fleet on the left. A mixed-instances policy can combine eligible instance types with On-Demand and Spot capacity. Diversification gives the allocator more options, but does not guarantee capacity.

Move to the requirements and image panel. Every selected instance needs a compatible AMI and software stack. When processor architectures differ, use suitable launch-template overrides and matching images rather than assuming one image boots everywhere.

Read the scale marked one unit and four units. Weights determine how each instance counts toward desired capacity. Define minimum, desired and maximum capacity in consistent units, and align scaling metrics with those units.

Inspect the design controls on the right. Choose the baseline On-Demand capacity, allocation strategy and interruption recovery together. Weighting changes capacity accounting; it does not choose the instance types by itself.

With the full slide visible, compare useful capacity rather than server count alone. Benchmark the workload, keep unit definitions consistent, and test recovery when a preferred instance pool is unavailable.
